findings.text: The first paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, so a newcomer can say what it is and why it matters within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: Someone visiting Athena's site meets a title about a different project, firstmate. Until they read the lede, it is unclear whether they are on Athena's home page or on a page about firstmate.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and h1 of the same text

findings.text: The lede names models, cost and verdict as what sets Athena apart, but this page never shows which models made the study, what it cost, or what the checking model concluded. The demonstration leaves out the features it advertises.
findings.source: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: The Next steps section is concrete: a clone command, the prerequisites, an install command and a first command to try. It is linked from the header, so the next action is easy to find.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ...", "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh", "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page promises two different models, but the prerequisites list only Claude Code. A newcomer can't tell where the second, checking model comes from or whether it needs its own account or key.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it" vs. prerequisites "either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: This link sits in the header with no explanation. A newcomer is not an owner and doesn't know what proposals it means, so it confuses them at the moment they are deciding whether to read on.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a state machine for firstmate, with exit codes, guards and 45 claims. That is too much detail for someone sizing up Athena. The 'Start here' section helps, but terms such as yolo, in scope, green and red are defined two or three times each.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (cards t1–t12), "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: Every claim links to exact file lines at a pinned commit, which shows the traceability Athena promises. A sceptical newcomer can check any sentence.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."

findings.text: The page is candid that nothing was run and that a first pass missed several paths. That honesty builds trust, but it also tells a newcomer the showcase is incomplete.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..." and f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: This section and the footer point to an internal repository folder. That means nothing to a first-time visitor and could be cut or explained.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
